01

Find the average needed on future assignments

The assignment average target calculator works backward from a desired final average. You provide the current mean, the number of completed assignments, and how many equal-weight assignments remain. It calculates the combined average required on that future work.

The key condition is equal final importance for every assignment in the calculation. This can describe a quiz category where each quiz counts once, or a course made entirely of equally weighted tasks. It does not describe a category in which larger point totals automatically count more. Confirm the rule before using the answer to decide what scores you need next.

02

Check both the average and the assignment counts

Enter your current assignment percentage average from zero to one hundred. Then enter whole-number counts for completed and remaining assignments. Both counts must be at least one. A count of three means three separate equal contributions, not three credits or three assessment categories with different weights.

Your current mean must represent exactly the completed count you enter. If four quiz scores include a recorded zero, both that zero and its quiz belong in the current average. Do not use an average calculated from three scores while entering four completed assignments. Excluded, excused, and ungraded items must be handled according to the instructor's rule rather than counted automatically.

03

Recover the existing score total, then solve the gap

Required future average = [Target × (Completed count + Remaining count) − Current average × Completed count] ÷ Remaining count.

Multiplying the current mean by the completed count reconstructs the total of the completed percentage scores. Multiplying the target by the final assignment count gives the combined score total needed. Their difference is the total percentage-score units required across the future assignments.

These units are a convenient arithmetic total, not course percentage points or raw earned marks. Dividing by the number of unfinished assignments converts the total back into an average percentage. The formula assumes no score is dropped and no assignment changes its weighting when another mark arrives.

04

Three completed assignments and two remaining

Suppose three assignments average 70%, and two remain. An 80% final average across five assignments requires a score total of 80 × 5 = 400. The completed scores contribute 70 × 3 = 210, leaving 190 for the last two. Dividing 190 by two gives a required future average of 95%.

That does not demand identical scores. A 90% and a 100% produce the needed 95% future mean. A 94% and a 96% do too. However, an 85% first future score would require 105% on the last assignment, which exceeds this model's score range. Recalculate as actual marks arrive rather than assuming the original target remains equally flexible.

Check the example in the forward direction: 70 + 70 + 70 + 90 + 100 totals 400. Dividing by five gives 80%. The three seventies represent the existing average, not necessarily the actual individual marks, but their total is equivalent.

05

Compare the influence of different remaining counts

If three completed assignments average 70% and only one remains, reaching 80% overall would require 110% on that last task. With two remaining, the requirement is 95%. With three remaining, it is 90%. More equal-weight work creates more opportunity to change the final mean.

The completed record also becomes harder to move as it grows. Ten assignments averaging 80%, followed by one score of 100%, produce 81.82% overall. The new perfect score raises the mean by about 1.82 points. This is why a large improvement on one task need not create an equally large movement in the displayed average.

06

Read the required minimum carefully

The calculator rounds the required average upward to two decimal places. A result above 100% is shown as Not reachable under the ordinary percentage limit. A result at or below zero displays zero because the current score total already supports the chosen target even with zeroes on the remaining tasks.

An average is a condition across the remaining group, not a minimum score for every task. The answer also does not enforce separate submission requirements or a minimum mark on a particular assignment. If the instructor requires every task to be completed, satisfying the arithmetic with some zeroes does not remove that requirement. Treat the output as one part of the course plan.

07

Avoid using this with unequal assessment weights

Equal maximum marks are not the only way to create equal weighting. An instructor might convert a ten-point quiz and a twenty-point quiz into percentages and then average those percentages equally. Conversely, two assessments with the same maximum can receive different final weights. The published averaging method settles which model applies.

If assignments have different course weights, use the weighted grade calculator. If several remaining tasks together form a fixed unfinished course share, use the remaining grade calculator. Do not combine a homework-category mean and an exam percentage here as though each were one assignment unless their final weights are genuinely equal. Dropping the lowest result also requires a different calculation.

08

Build a flexible assignment-by-assignment plan

Write down the remaining tasks and possible score combinations that meet the required mean. Include room for uncertainty rather than relying on a single ambitious mark. Review rubrics and feedback to identify where additional preparation could plausibly help, while giving each deadline enough attention.

Once another assignment is graded, update the current average and increase the completed count by one. Reduce the remaining count by one, then calculate again if at least one assignment remains. When all work is complete, use the ordinary grade average calculator to check the final mean. Keep a record of which marks were confirmed and which were only scenarios so estimates do not become confused with official results.

Quick answers

Frequently asked questions

Can the remaining assignments have different raw maxima?

Yes, but only if the instructor converts each to a percentage and gives each identical final weight. If raw points are pooled, an assignment with more available marks has more influence and this model is unsuitable.

Can I enter zero remaining assignments?

No. The calculation divides by the remaining count, so at least one unfinished assignment is needed. With no remaining work, there is no future average to solve; calculate the completed mean instead.

What if my current average was rounded by the gradebook?

The calculator reconstructs completed score totals from that rounded average, which can introduce a small error. Use the most precise available mean or calculate it from the underlying scores before planning a close target.

Does a required 95% mean I should aim for exactly 95%?

It is the mathematical minimum average under the entered assumptions. Your scores may be awarded in discrete increments, and course rounding can differ. Aiming above the boundary provides room for variation, but no score outcome is guaranteed.
